title: 48. Thiamine modulation of hepatocytes respiration.
content:
Abstract
As a precursor for a key metabolic coenzyme involved in fundamental energy metabolism and mitochondrial function, thiamine (vitamin B1) is a vital nutrient for all living organisms. We previously demonstrated that high-dose thiamine administration prevented experimental fatty liver in sheep (Kalyesubula et al., 2021); however, the cellular mechanism underlying this protective effect remains unknown. We hypothesized that thiamine reduces intrahepatic lipid accumulation by enhancing cellular fuel oxidation and mitochondrial respiratory activity. To test this, we employed a bioenergetic respiratory approach to assess the functional impact of thiamine on mitochondrial oxygen consumption rates in cultured hepatocytes. HepG2 cells were grown in either palmitate (0.2 mM) or glycerol (37%)-rich media and pretreated with or without thiamine hydrochloride (THC) at varying concentrations for 24 h. Oxygen consumption rates were assessed using a Seahorse XF Analyzer. Under palmitate exposure, THC-treated cells exhibited significantly higher basal (P = 0.0065), maximal (P < 0.0001), and ATP-linked respiration (P < 0.0001) compared with untreated control cells. Proton leak and mitochondrial coupling efficiency remained unchanged, indicating enhanced respiratory capacity without loss of efficiency. In contrast, under glycerol-rich conditions, THC treatment increased proton leak (P = 0.0085) and reduced mitochondrial coupling efficiency (P = 0.0003), consistent with mild, regulated mitochondrial uncoupling. Notably, non-mitochondrial respiration decreased under glycerol-rich but increased under palmitate-rich conditions following thiamine supplementation, suggesting enhanced peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation. Collectively, these findings indicate that thiamine modulates hepatocyte mitochondrial respiration in a substrate-dependent manner, i.e., enhancing oxidative capacity with fatty acid fuels, while promoting mitochondrial uncoupling with glycolytic substrates. This adaptive metabolic response provides mechanistic insight into thiamine’s protective effects against intrahepatic lipid accumulation and the development of fatty liver disease. References: Kalyesubula, M., R. Mopuri, J. Asiku, A. Rosov, S. Yosefi, N. Edery, S. Bocobza, U. Moallem, and H. Dvir. 2021.
